issues.legal_issue: A court charge is a fee rather than a tax when its primary purpose is to provide a special service to a defined class and its total collections broadly correspond to the total cost of that service.
material_facts: The challenged charge was imposed on litigants in connection with the administration of civil justice.
The State presented evidence of receipts from court fees and expenses associated with administering justice.
The Court found that the relevant relationship was between aggregate receipts and aggregate expenses, not the charge paid by an individual litigant and the service received by that litigant.
issues.conclusion: A broad and general correlation between total collections and total service costs is sufficient for the charge to retain the character of a fee; exact or individual-level equivalence is unnecessary.
issues.legal_principle: Under Entry 3 of List II of the Seventh Schedule, a legislature may charge fees for the administration of civil justice but may not use such a charge to raise general public revenue. The primary purpose must be a special service for a defined class, with broad aggregate correlation between collections and service costs. Exact arithmetic equivalence is unnecessary: I.M. & M. Industries v. State of Bihar; Government of Madras v. Zenith Lamps; Om Prakash v. Giri Raj Kishori; and P.M. Ashwanatha Narayana Setty v. State of Karnataka.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_court_charge: A litigant challenges the legal character or validity of a charge imposed in connection with court proceedings.
predicates.special_service_for_defined_class: The charge is primarily intended to fund a specific service provided to a defined class of persons.
predicates.broad_aggregate_correlation: The total amount collected bears a broad and general relationship to the total cost of providing the service.

issues.definition: When a challenged court charge funds a specific service for a defined class and aggregate collections broadly correspond to the cost of that service, the charge is a fee rather than a tax.

issues.legal_issue: A flat ad valorem court fee without an upper limit is not invalid merely because its incidence is disproportionate for particular litigants, if the fee satisfies the aggregate test for a fee.
material_facts: The challenged provisions imposed an ad valorem court fee at a flat rate without an upper limit.
The High Court had treated the burden on particular litigants as disproportionate and the fee as invalid.
The Supreme Court held that the constitutional character of the charge had to be assessed by comparing aggregate receipts with aggregate expenses, rather than by examining individual cases.
issues.conclusion: The absence of an upper limit and the disproportionate burden on some individual litigants did not, by themselves, invalidate the fee; the High Court's decision striking down the provisions could not stand.
issues.legal_principle: The test for whether a levy is a fee is applied to the totality of receipts and the totality of expenses, not to each contributor's individual payment or benefit. A broad aggregate correlation suffices even if distribution among contributors produces inequitable effects; an arbitrary distribution may raise a separate constitutional concern. The Court applied P.M. Ashwanatha Narayana Setty v. State of Karnataka and the latitude afforded to legislatures in economic regulation, subject to Article 14 of the Constitution.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_court_fee: A person challenges the validity of a fee imposed for court proceedings.
predicates.flat_ad_valorem_rate_without_ceiling: The fee is calculated as a fixed proportion of the amount in dispute and has no upper limit.
predicates.broad_aggregate_correlation: The total amount collected bears a broad and general relationship to the total cost of providing the relevant service.

issues.definition: An uncapped fee calculated as a fixed proportion of the amount in dispute is not invalid solely because its burden is disproportionate for some litigants when aggregate collections broadly correspond to service costs.

issues.legal_issue: The cost of administering justice may include expenses for judicial officers who perform both civil and criminal functions and for government law officers who form part of the justice-administration machinery.
material_facts: The State included expenses associated with criminal courts and government law officers in its account of justice-administration costs.
Judicial officers performing civil work also exercised magisterial powers and dealt with criminal matters.
The High Court had excluded some of those expenses when assessing the cost of civil justice.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was wrong to exclude those expenses categorically: the mixed functions of judicial officers made it difficult or impossible to separate civil and criminal costs, and government law officers were also part of the machinery of the administration of justice.
issues.legal_principle: For deciding whether court-fee receipts broadly correspond to the cost of administering justice, costs need not be divided with exact precision between civil and criminal functions where the same judicial officers perform both. Expenses for law officers may also be included when they form part of the machinery of justice administration. The Court relied on its discussion of the State's justice-administration responsibilities and All India Judges Association v. Union of India.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_court_fee: A person challenges the validity of a fee imposed for court proceedings.
predicates.judicial_officers_perform_mixed_function: The same judicial officers perform civil work and exercise criminal or magisterial functions.
predicates.law_officers_part_of_justice_machinery: Government law officers contribute to the machinery involved in administering justice.

issues.definition: Where judicial officers perform both civil and criminal functions and law officers contribute to justice administration, their associated costs may be counted in assessing the cost of administering justice.

issues.legal_issue: A court fee does not cease to be a fee merely because collections do not exactly match expenses in a particular year or because the State obtains an incidental surplus.
material_facts: The High Court found that receipts exceeded certain expenses in some years and treated the resulting surplus as evidence that the charge was a tax.
The State's evidence stated that it was difficult to estimate some justice-administration expenses precisely and that the High Court had not considered all the relevant material.
The Supreme Court held that fluctuations between receipts and expenses were inevitable and that exact annual matching was not required.
issues.conclusion: An annual surplus or lack of exact arithmetic correspondence does not invalidate a fee when its primary purpose is to provide a specific service and there is broad aggregate correlation between receipts and expenses.
issues.legal_principle: The correlation required for a fee is broad and general, not mathematically exact or necessarily established year by year. Incidental benefit to the State, including a surplus, does not change the levy's character when its primary purpose is to provide the specific service. The Court applied I.M. & M. Industries v. State of Bihar, Government of Madras v. Zenith Lamps, and P.M. Ashwanatha Narayana Setty v. State of Karnataka.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_court_fee: A person challenges the validity or character of a fee imposed for court proceedings.
predicates.approximate_cost_accounting: The expenses of providing the service cannot be allocated or calculated with exact precision, or collections vary from expenses over time.
predicates.broad_aggregate_correlation: The total amount collected bears a broad and general relationship to the total cost of providing the relevant service.

issues.definition: When cost accounting is approximate but aggregate collections broadly correspond to service costs, an annual mismatch or incidental surplus does not make the fee a tax.
